title: Query-Limited RAM Programs and their Applications
authors: Jiahui Liu, Justin Raizes, Bhaskar Roberts, Omri Shmueli
abstract: Quantum one-time programs (Broadbent, Gutoski and Stebila, CRYPTO 2013) or OTPs for short, enable a functionality to be encoded into a quantum token that can be evaluated on a single chosen input and then becomes unusable. While powerful, this primitive is inherently stateless and tied to a setting in which a quantum token needs to be issued and distributed for every single evaluation of a circuit. This raises a natural question: can the one-time computation paradigm be extended to richer, stateful forms of controlled access, and would such an extension offer inherent advantages beyond standard OTPs?   We introduce $\textit{query-limited RAM programs}$ (QLPs), a RAM-generalization of QOTPs that supports structured, stateful computation under bounded or policy-driven access. QLPs allow controlled sequences of evaluations while preventing adversarial forking or rollback of computational state. This enables new applications beyond stateless one-time programs, including quantum tokens for Turing Machines whose size depends only on $\textit{code length}$ (and not runtime), transferable $k$-time or budget-limited programs, and low-communication mechanisms for delegating computation in settings such as Software-as-a-Service.   To construct QLPs, we introduce $\textit{one-shot programs}$, unifying one-shot signatures (Amos, Georgiou, Kiayias and Zhandry, STOC 2020) with the single effective query paradigm (Gupte, Liu, Raizes, Roberts and Vaikuntanathan, STOC 2025). We prove that one-shot programs generically imply query-limited programs, demonstrating that the strengthened unclonability guarantees of one-shot signatures translate into enhanced functionality. Along the way, we clarify the relationship between signature-token primitives and quantum one-time programs via generic constructions, essentially showing that one-time signing programs imply one-time general computation.
summary: This paper advances the theory of quantum one-time computation by introducing Query-Limited RAM Programs (QLPs). QLPs extend stateless OTPs to support structured, stateful computation while preventing state manipulation. This work is significant for developing quantum tokens and secure delegation mechanisms for quantum computation.
main_problem: The paper addresses the need to extend the stateless nature of Quantum One-Time Programs (OTPs) to support richer, stateful, and controlled computation paradigms.
main_result: They introduce Query-Limited RAM Programs (QLPs), demonstrating that one-shot programs generically imply QLPs, enabling applications like quantum tokens for TMs whose size depends only on code length.
method: The authors develop a unified framework by generalizing OTPs into QLPs, which are constructed by unifying one-shot signatures with the single effective query paradigm.
model_or_system: The core models are Quantum One-Time Programs (OTPs) and the proposed Query-Limited RAM Programs (QLPs), which generalize the concept of one-time computation to support stateful access control.
key_observables: Controlled access, prevention of adversarial forking or rollback, and the dependence of token size on code length rather than runtime.
important_parameters: The degree of statefulness (stateless vs. stateful), the number of queries allowed, and the security strength derived from one-shot signatures.
main_assumptions: The security proofs rely on the existence and properties of one-shot signatures and the ability to construct QLPs from these primitives.
figures_summary: No specific figure summaries are available, but the notes mention conceptual protocols (e.g., Figure 16) illustrating the semi-quantum QLP protocol.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first identifying the limitation of stateless OTPs, then introducing QLPs as a generalization, and finally proving the relationship between one-shot signatures and QLPs through construction and implication proofs.
why_interesting: While highly theoretical, the concepts of controlled quantum access and stateful computation are fundamental to designing secure quantum protocols for future quantum computing infrastructure.
